title: Seeing the worthy
hookLine: seeing the worthy, think of equalling them; seeing the unworthy, examine yourself (Analects 4.17)
tomorrow: Confucius sums up his whole life in six lines. how does it end?

lines: THE ONE WHO CALMS THE CALLER.
THE ONE WHO SETS THE ROOM ON EDGE.
cards: A new hire learns more from watching than from the manual: how one coworker calms an angry caller, and how another sets the whole room on edge.

The Analects has a line for both, in Legge's translation: "When we see men of worth, we should think of equalling them; when we see men of a contrary character, we should turn inwards and examine ourselves."
Two later Confucian thinkers disagreed about human nature, and so about what happens inside us when we do this.

teach.h: MENCIUS: THE CHILD AT THE WELL.
teach.b: Mencius tells a story. Anyone who suddenly sees a small child about to fall into a well feels alarm, not to win the parents' favor or the neighbors' praise, just alarm.
For Mencius that flinch is a sprout: goodness is already in us, and seeing a worthy person waters what's there. Xunzi answers with a woodworker.

teach.h: XUNZI: WARPED WOOD ON THE FRAME.
teach.b: Warped wood only comes straight on the press frame, with steam and pressure. Human nature, he says, left alone runs to wanting and grabbing; goodness comes from effort, teachers and models.
For Xunzi, the worthy person is the frame.

Let both speak. Mencius: if goodness weren't in us, no example could wake it, and the child at the well shows it's there. Xunzi: if goodness were simply in us, why would anyone need teachers, rites and years of practice?

Here's what they share, and it's the teaching of the line: other people are your textbook, both kinds. The worthy show you who to become. The unworthy send you back to your own conduct, not to judging theirs.
One to tell a friend: the Analects doesn't say avoid bad examples. It says use them as a mirror.
Mencius and Xunzi would both say examine yourself. They disagree about what you'll find.

how: Confucian learning uses models: teachers, ancestors and worthy people to imitate. Readers of Analects 4.17 take an unworthy example as a cue for self-examination rather than judgment.

o: copy the worthy, and let the unworthy send you inward
admire good people and cut bad ones out of your life
judge others carefully before you trust their example

games.q: two readers, one line: tap the pairs.
p: goodness sprouts, like alarm at the well
goodness is made straight, like warped wood

s: the Analects says to stay away from bad examples
4.17 says to look at them, then turn inward and examine yourself.
Xunzi said goodness comes by effort, teachers and models
his picture is warped wood brought straight on the press frame.
Mencius said goodness has to be forced into us from outside
that's closer to Xunzi. Mencius saw sprouts of goodness already in us, like alarm at the well.

games.q: your friend sides with Mencius: goodness is already in us. steelman the other side: what's Xunzi's best case?
o: even good wood needs the frame: models and practice straighten us, so copy the worthy on purpose.
people are simply wicked, so trying to improve is pointless.
Confucius never mentioned learning from others, so copying isn't Confucian.
games.why: Xunzi isn't a cynic: his whole point is that people can become good, through effort, teachers and models. that's why he wrote about learning.

practice: Bring to mind one person you admire and one who rubs you the wrong way. With the first, find one thing you could copy this week. With the second, ask quietly where you do a smaller version of the same thing.

wordCard.voice: Seeing the worthy: let the good example pull you up, and let the bad one send you inward.

orig.note: Chinese xian, the worthy: the people Analects 4.17 says to think of equalling.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: examine myself, because another's fault is a mirror before it's a verdict. Talk tomorrow.

sources.q: When we see men of worth, we should think of equalling them; when we see men of a contrary character, we should turn inwards and examine ourselves.

sources.ref: Mencius 2A6 (the child about to fall into a well; the four sprouts)
Xunzi, ch. 23 'Human Nature Is Bad' and ch. 1 'Encouraging Learning' (warped wood and the press frame; goodness from conscious effort, teachers and models)
